utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Two administrative matters before we continue with the evidence. I'll ask the court registrar to give us the result of the work he did last night with the numbering of the medical records. Do you wish to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and to Your Honours. Something I meant to do last night after Your Honours' decision about the affidavit, and that is simply to offer it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I have the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the affidavit being put in evidence now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Please give that a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be admitted as number P48. Additionally, the documents listed in the affidavit will have the Exhibit numbers P49 through P82 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I understand the parties have been given a copy of the document showing the numbering.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next administrative matter relates to the filing of several motions for protective measures by the Prosecution, and two of those relate to two witnesses who are to testify next week. The motions were filed, the first one on the 17th of January, and the Defence response is due on the 29th of January, but Witness 35 is scheduled to testify on Monday morning. This immediately raises a problem of the lateness of the filing, Mr. Whiting, so I must ask in future that you ensure that sufficient time is given for the Defence to reply before the witness is brought to court. Of course, many of these matters are frequently dealt with, I don't want to say routinely, but dealt with in court and dealt with very quickly. So I'm going to ask the Defence whether you would be in a position to reply by tomorrow. If you can reply by tomorrow, by midday, then we can issue a decision on this in the afternoon, orally, and the witness can be brought in for Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. We are going to give you our opinion orally now, and it's an affirmative answer. Regarding the witnesses that are already planned, we don't want to create logistical problems for the Prosecution. I mean, we're in the same boat, after all. So we agree for those two witnesses. The Prosecution filed on January 11th another motion regarding the testimony of these witnesses, according to Rule 92 ter. I think this is Witness W83 and 36. So we agree for both of these witnesses. They can testify according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I take note of that. There is another motion for protective measures filed on the 18th of January relating to Witness 62, and there your response would be due on the 30th of January. Are you in a position to comment on that now?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Witness 62, is he also planned to testify in the week -- in the coming?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he is scheduled to testify on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately -- well, I have the list with me, but I have to look in my documents. Could I please look -- will you allow me a minute so I can look into my list, please, to see exactly who it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may inform us of that later so we can get on with the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what we'll do. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, just very briefly, Your Honour. First of all, I would apologise for the late filings. Of course, as Your Honour is aware, oftentimes these requests for protective measures come only when we start to schedule and bring the witness here, so that's -- and then we file it immediately, and so that's why that happens sometimes. But we will try to do our best to make sure that the Defence has enough time. Secondly, I'm extremely grateful to the Defence for the accommodation with respect to responding both to the protective measures motion and the 92 ter motion. It's an accommodation which we will remember and I think we'll probably have occasion to return when they're doing their case. Just for the record, the two witnesses, however, for the 92 ter it, it's 83 and 35, not 36, just so the record is clear. Those two witnesses are scheduled to testify on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I commend the parties for their spirit of cooperation. It's in the highest traditions of the bar. Now, may I ask the --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please. So we also agree for that witness. We just checked a minute ago. So for Witness VW62, we agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic now. And, Mr. Tapuskovic, you will have one hour to complete the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, and I hope that I will manage, and I must do my best to be as efficient as possible. I'm also grateful for your assessment, and I deem it to be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandilovic, my name is Branislav Tapuskovic, an attorney from Belgrade, a Defence counsel for Dragomir Milosevic. And I would like to ask you, regarding what we discussed yesterday, about certain things that you perhaps are able to tell us something from your direct experience or if you have secondhand knowledge; and, if possible, I'm kindly asking you to give me the briefest possible answers because time is the issue here. And as far as I understand, you are going to comply.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, will you reply orally, not just by nodding your head.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what was the answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told Mr. Tapuskovic that I'm going to do my best to comply with his requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had to revise the order of my questions, and I'm going to address something which is more important for the accused. That is a specific event that was just tackled somewhat yesterday, and it refers to the event which took place on the 8th of November, 1994 - that is item 1 in the indictment - and the first event described in the annex relating to the shelling. My initial questions will be focused on this particular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, yesterday you described, if I may say, your most difficult experience during the war that you survived. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I described the event yesterday in response to the Prosecutor's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain: How is it possible that this experience, which truly deserves to make others feel uncomfortable in the face of the gravity, how is it possible that you don't remember the date of such an event, if it was just a single event in which your life was threatened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date. There were so many similar events. There were so many hits that targeted the southern part of the hospital, but this one was unique because I was on that floor, and I was never before or after that closer to an explosion. That was the point. But otherwise, there were lots of similar situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So that was the hit on the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then I will curtail my questioning even more. The Prosecutor, according to the list of the documents that they intend to enter as evidence, specifically relating to the event of the 8th of November, 1994, they show you a set of documents.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of documents?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters are kindly asking the speakers not to overlap and to pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the interpreter is asking both the witness and yourself not to overlap. Please observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Item 3 in this list that concerns the event of the 8th of November, 1994, speaks about a criminal investigation that the Prosecution mentioned here and which, according to what I can see from this list, was something that you had probably been shown by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, but I did not mention a criminal investigation yesterday in my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He said you are misquoting, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible. Then I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know nothing about the event of the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen any document in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: You know nothing about the event and the shell that hit Livanjska Street and where some people were killed or injured?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you can't remember the date, did you have and opportunity to see someone brought into the hospital on the 8th of November as a casualty?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said I cannot remember the date, but believe me, for three and a half years people were being brought in permanently, and it is impossible to make difference and distinction between different weeks and months. People came from different parts of town, injured by shells, by grenades, by shrapnel. So even if I try my best, it is impossible to know exactly who and when came to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember or can you say that on that day, do you know at all that there was fierce fighting and shooting in Sarajevo and around?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. Maybe. Intense fighting was a very frequent occurrence, and there was shooting all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in front of me I have a document compiled by UNPROFOR which relates to that specific event of the 8th of November which shows exactly what transpired. If he, as a witness, cannot say anything about this but he confirms that there was fighting around that time, I believe that I can suggest in this connection and this time frame - and I know that the Prosecutor will object to this - but this is the event in which an investigation by the Bosnian police established that the projectile came from the Serbian positions - and I'm talking again about the event of the 8th of November - and UNPROFOR established quite the opposite; that the projectile was fired from inside the town from the positions of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned friend is correct about the objection. Firstly, the witness has not confirmed that he knows anything about an incident on the 8th of November. Secondly, when asked about intense fighting, his response was, "Maybe. Maybe. Intense fighting was a very frequent occurrence and there was shooting all the time." That's hardly a confirmation that there was fighting on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd agree with the Prosecutor that there would be no basis for further questioning along those lines. But if you wish to put the incident to the witness, let him look at the document and to see whether it refreshes his memory, then I have no objection to that. You may either just summarise the incident and ask whether his memory is refreshed as to it and see whether we can get any further, but let us do it quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: According to this report, and possibly there was some coverage in the press about that, according to this UNPROFOR report which was quite clear, the event took place on the 8th of November, 1994, at -- sorry, at 1725 hours. And in order to refresh your memory further, do you remember that on that same day another event took place, a very serious event which took place at 1530? Does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm sorry, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you must move on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honours, I'm going to move on. This is the document, but it will soon be put on the table again, and it will show what UNPROFOR had established. I do acknowledge that your objection is warranted and well placed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are not to give evidence, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'm not giving evidence, Your Honours. I'm going to use these documents later. I perfectly know that I'm not here to give evidence. Documents will speak about this event, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The next topic, Mr. Witness, would be these magical records that have been mentioned. I'm interested in one thing: Did you sign each and every record, and does that reflect your analysis, your diagnosis, and your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the documents that have been handed over?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have analysed all these documents, and I stand by it, that these are the records from the hospital in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But these are not the documents that you provided based on your analysis and your diagnosis. You only confirmed that you had received it from someone else, that it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And incidentally, among these about 100 documents, there are two documents that I personally compiled and wrote with my own hand 13 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So as for the others, you cannot confirm that they are 100 per cent acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that they are 100 per cent acceptable. And I know very well all the findings, and I recognise the handwritings of all the physicians who signed these records.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have just received a piece of information from the Prosecution yesterday, or the day before yesterday, which speaks about your account of an incident in which two persons were injured in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I described that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know their full names?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, but I think that this can be found in the medical records. However, at the moment I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that they were hit through the window.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were in the southern part of the hospital, facing the slopes of Trebevic, and they were hit by bullets from small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I will now move on to questions relating to the tram service that you described yesterday. Was there any difference in how the trams were being targeted with respect to these two periods? Because you had given two statements. Once you spoke about what I asked about you yesterday and the second time you spoke about the General Milosevic period. Was there any difference in how the trams were targeted between these two different periods?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tram service was reinstated in Sarajevo quite late. They ran along the east-west and west-east line. And the service was resumed rather late, and as far as I can remember it took place while the Dayton negotiations were very intensively going on. And when there was an official truce in place - and I remember then - these incidents did happen in that specific period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, the bus that you used, which route did it take? And if we can please have the map that we were using yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will show you on the map if it is precise enough. I will --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have map number 6 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I made an objection yesterday. I hope you would agree with that, that this is not a very clear and accurate map. It is very difficult to find here because there are no streets entered or plotted in the map. But I can tell you, I can describe to you, the route that this bus used to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you -- I would like this route that the witness is going to show be marked and that this be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there a number for this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I think there is an electronic form which the witness can mark. I'll have to confer about the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's map number 6. I'm going to ask the Prosecution to try and get a better map of Sarajevo. This one is admittedly not very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, we will try and do that. There is a map that I used yesterday which, I submit, is clearer than this one, which perhaps can be used. But if it is of some help, my case manager has advised me that the PT number is 2738.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can we have PT2738. That apparently is a better map. It's coming, I understand. It just takes a little time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This map that's on the -- or, rather, that's on our screens right now, is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this is. This is a map of Sarajevo, but this apparently is not what we need. I don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, return the original map to the witness and let him do the marking on that map, if he can, if he's able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps now that the map is in full screen the witness could do the markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we're back to the map which is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If it could be zoomed in, which would help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a better map. Now we have a much better situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is not the map that I need. It is difficult for me to get what I need. It is difficult for him to show.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'm sorry. I apologise. It's very easy to do here because you can see the hospital here and the road that I took toward the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then please do go ahead and show us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This here is the hospital. This would be the route, more or less, but you cannot now ask me to be completely accurate because this is a very small-scale map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be given a number immediately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please give it a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to ask the witness the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is more or less the same route --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's wait for the number from the registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be admitted as Exhibit D13.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is the route, precisely the route that the tram takes; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But is it parallel to it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is parallel, and let me show you because you apparently were not in Sarajevo. This was the so-called salvation route that went parallel to the main road here, but it went behind the Marshal Tito barracks and in front of the railway station. And as I mentioned yesterday, at all the crossroads there were large screens placed in order to safeguard the people against sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please tell me, while you took this route on the bus were you ever fired upon?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, in answer to the questions asked by the Prosecution, you said, if the interpretation was correct, that your hospital was in a location that was about 1.000 metres from the demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, less. Less than that. This is what I've already said. It was about 500 metres. You are a little bit mixed up, sir. We spoke about 1.000 metres in relation to the distance, as the crow flies, from the Markale market to the hospital; that would be 1.000 metres. And here I state that the hospital was about 500 metres away from the demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. In your statement that you gave to the investigators on the 11th of February, when asked whether this was more or less what you said, the distance was several hundred metres and that is why you had to move to the opposite side of the building to be away from the demarcation line. So you just moved within the hospital to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did two things. We had to do two things. First of all, all the patients and all the staff and all the equipment was moved to the lower floors or to the ground floor in the basement in order to be able to withstand the heavy artillery fire targeting the hospital. Later on, as the number of patients increased - and this is something we couldn't deal with - we were forced to put the less seriously ill people on the lower floors of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to waste too much time on these maps, but I do have to ask you the following: The location that you showed us as the place -- as the location where the hospital was, that was at this distance that you specified from the front line, does that mean that the hospital was -- the part of the hospital that was targeted, that it was actually facing the front line?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The main entrance of the hospital faced south.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You spoke about this yesterday - and I don't want to dwell on that - but let me ask you: The two points, Colina Kapa and Debelo Brdo, they are the two dominant points, and of course the hill of Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "the dominant points"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these are two hills, two -- one is almost a thousand metres high and the other is maybe 800. I can't remember the exact height. Would those be the hills that dominated the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on to a document. It's a document D001078. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not getting any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us how frequently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge Mindua. I got no interpretation. May I ask you to repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Yes, okay. [Interpretation] Witness, I was asking you to tell us how frequently the hospital was hit between the 10th of August, 1994, until the 21st of November, 1995, i.e., the relevant period in the indictment. How many shots were fired? Were there moments when there were fewer shots or more shots? Was it cyclical or did this happen in a random fashion? Could you expand on this a little bit, because we are particularly interested in this question. Of course, could you also tell us whether this was deliberate or not, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my testimony I said - and this is something that I maintain to this day - that in 1994 and 1995, in other words, the period that we're talking about, that it was a calmer period from the point of view of our work in the hospital. And since the hospital was part of the city itself, this means that the life in the city was calmer at this period. What I want to say is that in this period the targeting of the hospital and the city by artillery was less intense than in the previous period. However, we cannot say that the hospital was not targeted at all. There was shelling; there was rifle fire. I cannot state, as I sit here today, whether this was deliberate or not. It is a fact that the hospital was fired on, and this was documented. So we do not have to rely on feeble human memory. We have photographs to rely on, and this is an important historical document. Those photographs are a historical record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we have the document that I wanted on the screen, and now I would like to ask you something about the page 3 of this document, and it's page 3, last paragraph in the English version, too. Do you have this in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Third paragraph from the bottom, you say here: "As the war in Sarajevo drew ever closer, I knew that I would face a decision whether I should stay or go."

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "I was never under any pressure to make the decision, and in the end, in fact, we were informed that if we wanted to leave the State Hospital we could do so and we would not suffer any consequences."

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told this by the representatives of the Yugoslav People's Army, that you were a member at the time as a doctor in the medical corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in the next paragraph: "When the JNA withdrew from the State Hospital, I would not have any difficulties in returning to Serbia because I was a citizen of Yugoslavia. My decision was that I would stay in Sarajevo, which I did."

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by what I stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now in the third paragraph, that's the last one, you stated the following: --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- "Making this decision was difficult because remaining behind when your unit has left is, in effect, desertion."

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you go on to say: "As a professional soldier, this is a step that is not undertaken lightly. My decision to stay was based on two aspects." Yes? Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have not read the statement until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to make it easier for the interpreters. I will ask you about the remainder of the statement, but could you please tell me, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this correct. This is what I said; this is what I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Firstly, I'm a doctor and it's my duty to provide medical care, and that's why I stayed, for humanitarian reasons. Secondly, to leave would have been a journey into the unknown, which I was not prepared to undertake."

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I stand by what I stated at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words -- can I ask you yet another question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Had you gone, had you left, that would have meant that you would have gone into exile. You would have remained -- you would have been without your apartment, without your friends. It would have been a journey into the unknown. You would have become a refugee.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps, but this is not what I said. This is not what I said. It is possible that this might be the case, but this is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So this was something that was possible. Was this something that 110.000 people, Serbs, had to do? They had to leave. They had to leave their homes, their houses, their friends, and they also left behind quite a few of their relatives among the 40.000.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you an answer, although this is not related to medical matters. I don't know about the figures. The figures that you provide, I cannot comment on it. I know quite a few Serbs that stayed. A lot of them stayed. And I know that nobody was forced either to stay or to leave, so I cannot really agree fully with your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you agree to the fact that a lot of Serbs left immediately when the fighting broke out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite evident. I remember that. But not only Serbs. Let me be quite specific here. It is very important to note, in order to have a full picture of the events in 1992, April and May, a large number of Serbs left but a lot of Muslims left as well, Croats. And figures that I'm sure the international community has show that, about members of various ethnic communities in different countries, Germany, Austria, the United States, even Holland. So we must not be very narrow here. It was not just the Serbs that left. Everybody left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I never drew any distinctions in this respect, but let me ask you this: Is it true to say that it was mostly Serbs that left Sarajevo when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's difficult to say, but I do believe that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You lived in Sarajevo for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And people of all religions, beliefs, lived there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a town that was well-known for its tolerance, its tolerant atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you know that among those 40 or 50.000 people who stayed, they stayed although many of their closest relatives, fathers, children, had to leave, and they had to stay in Sarajevo. Do you know of any such cases?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I have to tell you the following: I worked in the hospital with a lot of Serbs. You can see that from the protocols and from the personnel files. But I don't know of any such cases, although this cannot be ruled out. So I couldn't really agree with this argument that you put forward now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So if that is the case, can you explain to me, please, you know that there were quite a few Serbs in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Without any strong military necessity, would the Serbian army shell Sarajevo even though they knew that some of them would be killed, that their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the witness is not in a position to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me move on now to direct issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going back again to this document. There is one thing that I would like to clarify together with you, and it refers to what is contained in the first paragraph on page 4 of the English version, where you say that the hospital was surrounded by the patriotic forces and that an agreement was reached that the defence will remain. How long did this siege or blockade of the hospital by the patriotic forces of Bosnia last?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my estimate, around a month. But I would like to be more accurate. This was not a classic siege. People were able to go in and out of the hospital. The hospital staff was able to come in and go out. There were only certain guards posted around the hospital that only controlled but did not prevent entry and exit. This is important to underline, because the word "siege" means something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any shooting at the hospital? Were there any JNA soldiers in or near the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were JNA soldiers towards the end of April and beginning of May in the hospital. That was, in fact, a unit of -- a special unit from Nis that came from airport Pleso in Zagreb. They came in order to defend the hospital. As far as I can remember, it was a 20-strong unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any clashes between them? Were there any casualties among the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't think so. As far as I can remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will need quite a lot of time to present my exhibits. Was it also true that all the barracks in town were under the blockade of members of the patriotic units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. As far as I can remember, yes. I wasn't in those barracks. I was in the hospital, but not until the very end. And I would like to underline that as well. I left the hospital on the 3rd of May, so I wasn't there at the moment when the hospital was handed over. But I know that there were barracks; I know that from the media and from other people's accounts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to get clarification as to the year, the exact year when the witness is talking about May and April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to that period as well, when the fighting began. I will obviously have to tender document DD00-1 ---

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 0166.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's, in fact, a document from the Federal Secretariat for National Defence addressed to the Presidency of BH. It's currently being translated. It's a very short document, and I would just like to read one sentence to the witness in order for me to be able to continue my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, and let the witness see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask the witness one thing concerning this document, where it says:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Understandably" - that's the third paragraph - "Understandably, it is necessary to ensure the adherence to what we agreed at the meeting in Skopje."

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's paragraph three on page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd just like to know the basis of -- you know, how this witness is being shown this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely what the witness said about all the barracks in town being surrounded by the patriotic forces, and I think an explanation was required what these patriotic forces were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were Territorial Defence forces of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's a different matter. What is written in this letter, that the barracks were surrounded, is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in any of the barracks, Mr. Defence Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You gave me a good reply, that you heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness has said he wasn't in the barracks, so he's not able to confirm the proposition that you put.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he heard about it secondhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the same thing happen to the barracks as happened to the State Hospital, i.e., that it was surrounded by the patriotic forces for almost a month? Did the same thing happen with other facilities in the city of Sarajevo, primarily the military facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it for myself, but I believe that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am kindly asking you - and I think that we are having technical problems for which I'm absolutely not to blame - to take into account when you decide on what time I will be allocated for my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any technical problems that have hindered your cross-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic. Please proceed. By my reckoning, you have another seven -- 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we wasted, certainly, seven or eight minutes with this map, and I believe that surely, under such circumstances, I will find it difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll give you another five minutes to those 10, in light of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just received a suggestion from the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This State Hospital was, in fact, a military hospital at that point in time when these things were happening, and it was precisely surrounded as a military facility.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never denied that. It was a military hospital, and it was under the control of the BH Territorial Defence. It was not surrounded, because surrounding is something different and controlling a facility are completely different things. People came freely in and out to be examined; nobody checked them. But it was under certain supervision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were soldiers able to leave?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, they were free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are unable to interpret this overlapping conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, Dr. Mandilovic and Mr. Tapuskovic, the interpreters are having difficulty because you're overlapping. You speak the same language, so please observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. I apologise, Mr. President. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although there are lots of things to be covered, a lot of ground to be covered, I will have to move on to another document, DD000192.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This, unfortunately, was something which we received but were completely unable to prepare ourselves, and that is why my cross-examination is taking as long as it is taking. This is his statement given on the 5th of January of this year, and we were totally unable to discuss it with the accused or to draw certain parallels between the two statements, which caused terrible difficulties for the Defence in examining this witness. I will try in a few minutes to wrap this up, if it is possible, and to clarify these two things and draw parallels between the two statements that we received on the very eve of the beginning of this trial. And it was totally impossible to check anything. I can finalise my examination on condition that we are being allowed to consult and confer with our client, and at any other time, when Mr. Mandilovic is available, I would like for him to come again because this is not the way to do the cross-examination properly, in the time that is allocated to us. And that is why I'm facing these difficulties. It's up to you to take a decision on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why are you only raising this matter now, Mr. Tapuskovic? Why are you now only informing the Chamber that you only received a second statement on the eve of the trial? Proper management would have dictated that you should have brought this to the attention of the Chamber before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I raised this issue yesterday about the time, and I counted on that I would have enough time and didn't want to cause any problems. But that was the first issue that I raised yesterday, that his statement was given via videolink which had put us in a situation where we could not highlight the basic things and to draw parallels and comparisons between the statements. In one statement he spoke about one period; in the second statement he spoke about the General Milosevic period. And that is what created all these troubles for us, and I did raise it at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already moved to this statement. I'll have to adhere to that. And whenever you say that I should finish, I will finish. And it seems that I won't be able to ask a whole series of questions that I had originally intended to. But let me ask him at least this:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke about a lot of things that had changed in comparison to the time that you described.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the years of 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm particularly interested in the period which is the summer of 1995 and the events that happened in summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that yesterday and earlier, that the year 1995 was the year in which the population of the city was very much exhausted and fatigued and psychologically totally devastated. But I can say one other thing, that the year 1995, compared to the previous years of war, was calmer. There were longer periods of cessation of fire that were agreed. Thanks mostly to the pressure of the international community, there was more food because the routes were opened. But I never said - and I confirm that today - that there weren't any serious fighting and that there weren't any serious shelling of the city of Sarajevo. In my statement, if you remember I mentioned yesterday two events that took place in 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not what I was asking you. You didn't answer my question. My attention was focused in my question on the summer of 1995, primarily May, June, and July, because I would like to hear something about that period because that is the only thing left to me to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that period, the most striking memory that I have, that is, the early summer of 1995 - and I said that yesterday as well - is the date the 16th of June, 1995, the dawn of that day, when an attempt started to lift the blockade by the forces inside the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did that take place after a relatively good period? Did you know that there was truce in force since January?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. These military and political documents were not available to me in my position, and I couldn't have known that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in the summer of 1995, could you see that there was shooting from both sides and that it started as you described it started, that the fierceness of the shooting was equal and even?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say. I was in a specific location, and the ring around Sarajevo was about 60 kilometres long. I couldn't tell you who started shooting and when shooting started. I'm not a competent person to discuss that. Nor was I present there, nor was I in a position. The only thing that I can tell you is that on that specific date, terrible destinations were heard in town; a large number of shells landed in the town. Both on the 16th, the 17th, and the 18th of June was the period of intensive shelling of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know about what happened at the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb side? I don't know how I could tell you anything about what was happening at the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in paragraph 14 -- when I asked you, you said you didn't know anything about political and military events. But did you say in paragraph 14 of this document -- perhaps we can call find it here. That would be page 4, but it's marked as paragraph 14 anyway. I can see this paragraph on our screens. You said that there was talk of peace and that everybody was hoping there would be peace and then this offensive was launched.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the 14th -- paragraph 14? It says here I was on duty whilst the attack on Markale was made. At first we in the hospital were all really shocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this peace. You say, "By this time the people were exhausted by the war. There was talk of peace." This is what I'm asking you about. And then the events of the summer followed.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the matter. We will allow you to go to the break if you need that time. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was just going to inquire. The question seemed to talk about the 16th of June, and paragraph 14 that's being referred to refers to, as the witness said, the Markale incident, which was in August 1995. So if I could elicit some clarity from counsel about the time period, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the date that you're addressing, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the entire summer of 1995. I know what happened at Markale. And I would like to say one thing once again, Your Honours. I will not say this again: When I deal with documents, because we are stretched for time, I don't want the witness to read the whole document and then to examine him. I'm focusing on the elements that are of interest to me. And if something is not the way I put it to the witness, the Prosecution always has the time to correct this, to deal with this in the re-examination. This, however, infringes on my right to the cross-examination. If I misquote something, if I did something wrong, the Prosecution has to deal with it in the re-examination. I did not misquote the witness at all. This is about Markale. But my question to the witness was that in the same paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me just say something in relation to that. Re-examination has a particular purpose, and any party has a right to object to a question being asked. It doesn't necessarily follow that the question relates to a matter that is to be dealt with in re-examination. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Paragraph 14 says that. "By 1995 the people were exhausted by the war. There was talk of peace." This is what it says here, and then -- is it true that there was this talk of peace, that people were saying, "Well, we will have peace soon"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People sincerely wanted to have peace, but for all intents and purposes there was no peace until the Dayton Peace Agreement came into force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you said that there was talk of peace.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that for four months there was a cessation of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I don't agree with what you say about the four months of peace. This is something that I cannot agree with, because it was completely impossible to have such a long period of peace in the besieged town of Sarajevo. You would have maybe a couple of days of cease-fire and then the hostilities would escalate and the international community would intervene; then there would be more escalation. Four months, it's a very long time period. And I absolutely do not agree with your estimate, with what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So what you said here, that there was talk of peace in this period, this is not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, but it doesn't mean that there was peace. Do you see the difference? Do you know what I mean? The people were following the reports in the media, because there were many international observers and reporters in Sarajevo. Sarajevo was, in fact, the centre of the world. There was a lot of pressure there. People were talking about the need for peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened. All I know is that there was some fighting, an escalation, and then it was later on from the media, domestic and foreign, we learned that there was an attempt to lift the siege of Sarajevo. But this is something that I didn't know at the time because I moved in very limited circles and my contacts were limited. And now you're asking me questions that belong to the highest military and political spheres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, do you now want to tell me that now my time is up? So do I still have a couple of more minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I said earlier that we'd allow you to go to the break, which is at 3.45 - that's another seven minutes - if you need that time. If you don't, we'll proceed with the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the documents that I've shown the witness, you said that it was -- the situation with the water and power improved a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in this period the water supply system from the Neretva functioned quite well, the cable?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know about that. This is not something that I was acquainted with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that in this period, from the end of 1994 and then onwards, the parties that had the greatest need for power, there were no power cuts. This is what President Izetbegovic said.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who said what. I just know the situation that I faced either as a citizen in my own home or in the hospital as an employee. But I did not move in those circles and I could not really give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I received hundreds of pages appended to your statement. They were -- all these documents were in Serbian, and of course there's no chance for me to be able to tender any of them. But there is a document that pertains to early 1995, and it is stated there that most of the problems with the power were caused by the very harsh weather conditions, because there was a lot of snow in this year, and that this was the main reason for the power cuts. The power installations, there were a lot of -- they were out of order most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tender this document through some other witness, but I merely wanted to focus on this period 1995 that the grid would break down. I can see that the Prosecutor seems to be on the verge of objecting, as if this is something that is not correct, but I'm asking you whether you are aware of this or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, the UNPROFOR can give you the best possible answer to that, because they monitored the situation all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This thing that I said is something that I read in a document that originates -- that was drafted by the technical staff and the civilian staff, civil servants of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I maintain what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I can't decide between the two alternatives. It would really be difficult for me to choose among the dozen or so questions that I still have, so let this conclude my cross-examination and let this be my responsibility for any prejudice that this might cause to my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No questions in re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Mandilovic, I would like to put a question to you, the purpose of which is to find out what seems to be the issue at stake here. From the last part of the Defence counsel's cross-examination, there seems to be an uncertainty as to the conditions in Sarajevo in the spring, the first half, at least, of 1995. And I do find that there is some unclarity in the statements that you have offered, because on the one hand you did say at a certain time that you thought that 1995 was the best and the calmest year compared to the preceding years. So I'm left with the impression that actually things became quite good, at least in the first half of 1995. Then on the other hand you also mention that on your birthday, I believe, on the 16th of June, the Bosnian army's attempt to break out began, and that this did cause some retaliation from the other side. And we have also spoken about the Markale 2 incident that occurred in August. So my question to you is: Have I understood you correctly when you say that at least until the summer of 1995, the situation in Sarajevo was more quiet, more calm, than in the previous year? And when I ask you this question, I do understand that at no time were there no hostilities. They were constantly shelling and firing, but it was on a general level, less aggressive in the spring of 1995 than it used to be the previous year. Can you elaborate a little on this question, sir. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, with what you say, with your assessment of the situation, and I stand behind what I said. It is my assertion that 1995 was, for all us in the besieged town of Sarajevo, much easier to bear. But I personally like what you have just said, that there was fighting all the time in the town. That is a fact. I merely wanted to compare 1992 and 1993 with the end of 1994 and 1995. If you compare these two time periods, certainly the latter two years were very much easier than the previous two. That is for sure. But at no point in time did the danger cease to exist. If you wanted to survive, you had to abide by certain rules, the rules that had been in existence for a long time. There was a shortage of everything. Your Honour, I've already spoken about this, but let me be quite specific. I spoke about the Blue Routes. They did open, but then they would close down again for reasons that are unknown to me. And when they were open, we would get a little bit more food and a little bit more medical supplies. But there were no Blue Routes in 1992 and 1993. We had no contacts with the outside world. But I think that you actually hit the nail on the head here. There was fighting at all times. It's just that there would be longer lulls between two bouts of fighting. And if you look at it in terms of percentages, there would be a larger percentage of peaceful days in the latter period than in the former one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, that concludes your evidence and you may now leave. In fact, we are now going to take the break, and we will resume with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Please be seated, sir. Sir, may I ask you to begin by stating your name.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: My name is Thorbjorn Overgard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Mr. Overgard, what is it that you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I'm a major in the Norwegian Air Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: What sorts of things do you do right now in the Norwegian Air Force?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I'm the commanding officer of an air base, NATO's most northern air base.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And how old were you when you joined the armed forces of Norway?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I was 17 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: When you joined the armed forces, which particular branch of the service did you join - the army, the navy, or the air force?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I started with the army, in the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: How many years were you an infantryman before you switched to the air force?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I was six, seven years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And what year was it that you switched over to the air force?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Have you been in the air force continuously since 1982?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Some questions, sir, about your education. Did you attend a formal university?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No. I have the war academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And what place, just briefly, does the war academy play in the training of Norwegian military officers?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: It's the main school to get you prepared for the duties you are going to do and to get, you could say, to be a regular officer and then start your career.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: So if I understand properly, to be a career commissioned officer, one must attend the war college?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: How long does the war college last?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: For one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Now, through your military background and experience, have you become familiar with various infantry small arms?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a type of ammunition that's often referred to it as 7.62-millimetre ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: To begin with, could you tell Their Honours what those numbers, 7.62, refer to.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: 7.62 is the case of the bullet. It's the length of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: All right. And what sorts of guns would fire 7.62-millimetre -- not highly specific, but, in general, what sorts of guns are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Small arms for infantry soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Are you also familiar with a type of ammunition referred to as 12.7-millimetre?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And, again, does the 12.7 refer to the length of the bullet's case?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: All right. What sorts of weapons fire 12.7-millimetre ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: It used to be only the machine-guns, heavy machine-guns, but lately we have seen sniper rifles with 7.62 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Isailovic is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but this is extremely fast. The interpreters are rushing. The witness and Mr. Docherty are both English speakers and everything is extremely fast. And the French translator is doing her best, but it is extremely fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll ask the counsel and the witness to speak a little more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I take the point, Your Honour, because we're both English speakers. I was not aware of the problem. I will slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Major Overgard, as an air force officer, are you also familiar with the types of ordnance that can be dropped from or fired from aircraft?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Before October of 1994, had you ever worked as -- the abbreviation is UNMO, United Nations Military Observer [Realtime transcript read in error "Owner"]?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No, I have not. I joined an UNMO course in Finland in May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: When you say that you joined an UNMO course in Finland, what was this Finnish course about?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: It is a course especially for educating UNMOs from Scandinavia mostly, but all other UN countries are also present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And during time of war, what is the job of an UNMO?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: It is to observe, investigate and to report, and we're reporting directly to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Is this dangerous work?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes. You are unarmed and you are living in villages together with the people, in the war area. And we are facing the same problems as the people in the villages are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At line 13, the question, there's a reference to "military owner." It should be "military observer." It's on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Did you serve, Major Overgard, as an UNMO in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: In what part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I started special training in Zagreb and then I was sent to Sarajevo, after 10 days -- six days in Zagreb. It was just testing about if I had the necessary UNMO skills.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And when? What were the dates that you started and ended working as an UNMO in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I arrived in Zagreb the 22nd of October, 1994, and we left Zagreb again the 3rd of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Did you volunteer to work as an UNMO or did the Norwegian Air Force order you to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I volunteered. I thought that was an interesting duty and I wanted to see how I functioned also during war activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask a couple of more questions about the training you undertook in Finland early -- in the first half of 1994. Can you tell us, please, what sorts of topics were covered in the curriculum of this Finnish UNMO course.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: It was investigation of various types of events, accidents, shooting, and this crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: When you say "crater analysis," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: It is craters after mortar and heavier weapons. I don't remember especially the name for it, but when it comes to weapons going up and coming down again, fired from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And how long was the Finnish UNMO course from start to finish?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: It was three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Of those three weeks, how much was devoted to crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: We had a lot of training in that, several different exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And what is the point of analysing a crater? When one analyses a crater, what questions is one seeking the answers to?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: It is to find the origin and try to establish where it was fired from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: After completing this course, did you feel competent to analyse craters?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: When you got to Bosnia, did you, in fact, analyse craters?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, and a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: A lot of them. Did you ever feel handicapped in the work you did in Bosnia by any lack of rigor or thoroughness in the Finnish course?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And you've told us the date on which you arrived in the Balkans. When was it that you arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I arrived in Sarajevo then around the 30th, I believe it was, the 22nd -- yeah, around -- I don't remember the date just now, but it was late October.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Late October --

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Where were you stationed when you first arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I was first stationed into a team called Sierra Whisky 1. It was a Blue 3 team outside Sarajevo on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And how long did you remain at Sierra Whisky 1?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Approximately 10 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: From your service, are you familiar with the geography of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: All right. And could you locate on a map the positions at which you were stationed?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, if I could please ask that Exhibit -- 65 ter number 2823 be displayed on the monitor to the witness and the courtroom personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let that be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Do you see that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No. I have no map in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it takes a little time. After Sierra Whisky 1 were you moved to another location?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, we were. They needed people or new UNMOs in Sierra Sierra 2, I think it was called, before Christmas, and me and a Dutch man were placed into Sierra Sierra 2, in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Now, you're being handed a silver pen, and with that silver pen -- first of all, is the map that's on the monitor a map of Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Can you find your location on that map and mark it with the pen.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes. We were somewhere in these houses. It has to be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Where the red dot appears?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Can I ask you, just so that it's easier to see, to circle that red dot. It's rather small.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes. In this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. What side of the confrontation lines was Sierra Whisky 1 on?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: It's on the -- it's the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I meant the one in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Sierra Sierra 2 was a pocket south of the airport in Sarajevo, the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Now, you were at the post on the Serbian side for a relatively short time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Why were you on the Serbian side for only, I think, nine or ten days?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: They had no other place to put us when we came, and as people are leaving - it's a team of people from all nations - and that's why after 10 days I was transferred to Hrasnica. We were also in this team two Norwegians, so that is not by the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: People should be of different nationalities on a team?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, may I ask that the image on the screen be frozen and given a P number and entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be admitted as P83.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 1st of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: During your time in Hrasnica, which was approximately seven months?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: During your time in Hrasnica, did you investigate incidents of sniping?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Did you investigate incidents of shelling?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Did you investigate incidents concerning air bombs?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
